public.prompt: A delivery-time dataset has a long tail trailing to the right. How does that affect the mean compared with the median?

options.text: The mean sits above the median
The mean sits below the median
The mean equals the median
The tail has no effect on the mean or median

opt_mean_above.message: Correct. The mean is more affected by extreme observations in the long tail, so it gets pulled toward the right tail, sitting above the median.

opt_mean_below.message: Not quite. A right-skewed distribution has a tail trailing to the right, which pulls the mean toward the right, not the left. The mean sits above the median, not below it.

opt_mean_equal.message: Not quite. The mean and median are equal only in symmetric distributions. In a right-skewed distribution, the mean is pulled toward the long tail, so it sits above the median.

opt_no_effect.message: Not quite. The tail does affect the mean: extreme observations in the long tail pull the mean toward them. The median is more robust to these extremes.

correct.message: Exactly right. The mean is pulled toward the long tail, while the median stays more centered.

incorrect.message: Remember: the mean is more affected by extreme values than the median.

hints: Think about which measure—mean or median—is more affected by extreme values.
The tail trails to the right, meaning there are some unusually high values. Which measure gets pulled toward them?

public.intro: The table shows 20 delivery times in minutes, sorted from fastest to slowest. Examine the spread of values to identify the distribution's shape.

tasks.prompt: Select the row with the extreme value that forms the long tail of this distribution.
Select a row near the start of where most values cluster (the bulk of the distribution).
Select a row near the end of where most values cluster (before the tail begins).
Select the cell showing the delivery time closest to the median — the value that would be the balance point if this distribution were symmetric.
Select the cell showing the delivery time that makes this distribution right-skewed — the extreme value in the long tail that also pulls the mean above the median.

task_tail_direction.correct: Correct. The 52-minute delivery at ORD-118 is the extreme value that forms the long tail trailing to the right.
task_tail_direction.incorrect: Not quite. Look for the value that is furthest from the bulk of the data—the extreme value that creates the tail.

task_bulk_start.correct: Correct. Around 20 minutes is where most delivery times begin to cluster.
task_bulk_start.incorrect: Not quite. Look for where the majority of values start to concentrate, not the absolute minimum.

task_bulk_end.correct: Correct. Around 30 minutes is where the bulk of values ends before the tail begins.
task_bulk_end.incorrect: Not quite. Look for where the concentration of typical values ends, before the values start trailing off.

task_shape_label.correct: Correct. The 52-minute delivery at ORD-118 is the extreme value in the right tail that makes this distribution right-skewed and pulls the mean above the median.
task_shape_label.incorrect: Not quite. Look for the value that stretches furthest to the right — the extreme value that creates the right tail, labels this distribution as right-skewed, and pulls the mean above the median.

task_symmetric_check.correct: Correct. 29 minutes (ORD-104) is the closest value to the median of 29.5 min — the balance point around which a symmetric distribution would trail off equally in both directions.
task_symmetric_check.incorrect: Not quite. A symmetric distribution trails off by roughly equal amounts in both directions from its centre. Look for the value closest to the midpoint of the data.

correct.message: Well done! You've identified the extreme value in the tail, the bulk of the distribution, and recognised that this distribution is right-skewed with the mean pulled above the median by that extreme value.

incorrect.message: Review the values carefully. Sort them mentally to find the extremes and the middle.

hints: Sort the delivery times from smallest to largest to find the extremes and middle values.
The extreme value in the right tail is what labels this distribution as right-skewed and pulls the mean toward the tail side.

public.prompt: You spot a delivery time of 80 minutes in a batch where most deliveries take 18–28 minutes. What should you do first?

options.text: Examine the record to see if it's a data error or a genuine event
Delete it immediately because it's an outlier
Ignore it and calculate statistics without checking
Replace it with the median value

opt_examine.message: Correct. You should examine the outlier to judge whether it's a possible data error or a genuine observation. A genuine outlier should not be removed without a very good reason.

opt_delete.message: Not quite. An outlier is not automatically a data error—it may be a genuine, correct observation. You should examine it first before deciding what to do.

opt_ignore.message: Not quite. Examining outliers is important: they can reveal data errors, interesting properties, or strong skew in the distribution. You should investigate before proceeding.

opt_replace.message: Not quite. Replacing an outlier without examining it first could hide a genuine observation or mask a data error that needs correction. Always investigate first.

correct.message: Exactly. Always examine an outlier before deciding how to handle it.

incorrect.message: Remember: an outlier might be a genuine observation, not necessarily an error.

hints: Think about what an outlier could represent—is it always an error?
What's the first step before making any decision about unusual data?

public.instructions: The table shows delivery times for seven orders. Flag any values that appear extreme relative to the rest of the data, and classify each: if only a data error is plausible choose 'Possible data error'; if only a genuine event is plausible choose 'Genuine event'; if both explanations are plausible choose 'Both possible — needs investigation'.

issues.explanation: The 80-minute delivery is extreme relative to the rest of the batch (18–28 min). It could be a data-entry error (e.g. 8.0 typed as 80) or a genuine event such as a road closure. Both explanations are plausible; the record must be examined before any decision is made.

decoys.message: 26 minutes is within the typical range (18–28 minutes) and is not an outlier.
28 minutes is at the upper end of the typical range but is not extreme relative to the rest of the data.

grading.wrong_category_message: You've identified the outlier, but a single explanation is not enough. The 80-minute value could be a data-entry error or a genuine event — both are plausible, so the correct response is to flag it as needing investigation, not to commit to one explanation without checking the record.
grading.completion_message: Well done! You've identified the extreme value and recognised that both a data-entry error and a genuine event are plausible explanations — the record must be examined before deciding.

correct.message: Excellent work. You've identified the extreme value and recognised that both a data-entry error and a genuine event are plausible explanations — the record needs examination before any action is taken.

incorrect.message: Look for a value that appears extreme relative to the rest of the batch.

hints: An outlier is an observation that appears extreme relative to the rest of the data.
Compare each delivery time to the others. Which one stands out as unusually high or low?

public.prompt: What is the table of counts of observations in each bin, which a histogram displays as bars, called?

options.text: A frequency table
A distribution table
A bin table
A count table

opt_frequency_table.message: Correct. The table of counts of observations in each bin is called a frequency table.

opt_distribution_table.message: Not quite. While the table does show the distribution of values, the specific term for the table of counts in each bin is 'frequency table.'

opt_bin_table.message: Not quite. While the table does organize data into bins, the standard term for the table of counts in each bin is 'frequency table.'

opt_count_table.message: Not quite. While the table does show counts, the standard term for the table of counts in each bin is 'frequency table.'

correct.message: Exactly right. A frequency table shows the count of observations in each bin.

incorrect.message: Think about the standard statistical term for a table that shows how frequently values appear in each bin.

hints: The term relates to how frequently observations appear in each bin.
This is a standard term in statistics for tables that show counts by category or bin.

public.intro: The frequency table shows delivery times grouped into bins, with the count of orders in each bin.

tasks.prompt: Select the row with the modal bin (the bin with the most observations).
Select the cell showing how many orders are in the modal bin.
Select the row with a bin that has zero orders.

task_modal_bin.correct: Correct. The 20–30 min bin has 9 orders, the highest count, making it the modal bin.
task_modal_bin.incorrect: Not quite. Look for the bin with the highest order count—that's the mode.

task_modal_count.correct: Correct. The modal bin has 9 orders.
task_modal_count.incorrect: Not quite. Find the bin with the most orders and select the cell showing that count.

task_empty_bin.correct: Correct. The 50–80 min bin has zero orders.
task_empty_bin.incorrect: Not quite. Look for a bin where the order count is 0.

correct.message: Excellent! You've read the frequency table correctly and identified the modal bin and the empty bin.

incorrect.message: Review the order counts in each bin. The mode is where the count is highest.

hints: The modal bin is the one with the tallest bar in a histogram—the highest count in the table.
Look at the order_count column to find the highest value and the zero value.

public.prompt: QuickShip data shows that as distance_km increases, delivery_minutes also tends to increase. What kind of association is this?

options.text: Positive association
Negative association
No association — the variables are unrelated
Causal relationship — distance causes longer delivery

opt_positive.message: Correct. When higher values of one variable tend to go with higher values of the other, that is a positive association.

opt_negative.message: Not quite. A negative association means higher values of one variable tend to go with lower values of the other. Here both distance and delivery time increase together, so the association is positive.

opt_no_assoc.message: Not quite. The variables do move together — farther orders tend to take longer. That is a positive association, not no association.

opt_causal.message: Not quite. Correlation describes the direction of an association, not causation. The correct term for this pattern is a positive association.

correct.message: Right. Higher distance tends to go with higher delivery time — that is the definition of a positive association.

incorrect.message: Remember: positive means both variables tend to move in the same direction; negative means they move in opposite directions.

hints: Think about whether the two variables move in the same direction or opposite directions.
In a positive association, higher values of one variable tend to go with higher values of the other.

public.prompt: A scatter plot shows a clear U-shaped curve between two variables, yet the computed correlation coefficient is close to 0. What does this tell you?

options.text: There is no relationship between the two variables
Correlation only captures linear relationships; a strong nonlinear relationship can still produce a near-zero value
The relationship is weak because the correlation is near 0
The correlation was calculated incorrectly

opt_linear_only.message: Correct. Correlation quantifies the strength of a linear relationship only. A nonlinear relationship can be strong even when its correlation value looks weak.

opt_no_rel.message: Not quite. The U-shaped curve is a clear relationship — it is just nonlinear. Correlation near 0 means little or no linear relationship, not no relationship at all.

opt_weak.message: Not quite. The relationship is strong — it is just nonlinear. Correlation near 0 only means the linear component is weak; it says nothing about nonlinear patterns.

opt_error.message: Not quite. The calculation is correct. Correlation near 0 for a U-shaped pattern is expected because correlation only measures linear association.

correct.message: Exactly. Correlation measures only linear association; a strong nonlinear pattern can still yield a near-zero correlation.

incorrect.message: Recall that correlation is limited to linear relationships. A near-zero value does not rule out a strong nonlinear pattern.

hints: What kind of relationship does the correlation coefficient measure?
A U-shaped curve is a nonlinear pattern. Does correlation capture nonlinear patterns?

public.intro: The table shows pairwise Pearson correlation coefficients for three QuickShip variables. Use it to answer the tasks below.

tasks.prompt: Select the cell showing the strongest linear relationship between any two different variables (highest absolute value, excluding the diagonal).
Select the cell showing a negative association between package_weight_kg and delivery_minutes.
Select the cell showing the weakest relationship between any two different variables (lowest absolute value, excluding the diagonal).

task_strongest_pair.correct: Correct. The distance_km / delivery_minutes correlation is 0.82, the largest absolute value in the matrix.
task_strongest_pair.incorrect: Not quite. Compare the absolute values of all off-diagonal cells and pick the largest.

task_negative_pair.correct: Correct. The package_weight_kg / delivery_minutes correlation is -0.41 — negative, meaning heavier packages tend to have slightly shorter delivery times.
task_negative_pair.incorrect: Not quite. Look for the cell in the package_weight_kg row (or column) for delivery_minutes and check its sign.

task_weakest_pair.correct: Correct. The distance_km / package_weight_kg correlation is -0.38, the smallest absolute value among the off-diagonal pairs.
task_weakest_pair.incorrect: Not quite. Compare the absolute values of all off-diagonal cells and pick the smallest.

correct.message: Well done. You read the sign for direction and the absolute value for strength across all three pairs.

incorrect.message: Focus on the absolute value for strength and the sign for direction. The diagonal (1.0) is each variable with itself — skip those.

hints: Ignore the diagonal (1.0 values). Compare the absolute values of the remaining cells to rank strength.
A negative sign means the two variables move in opposite directions; a positive sign means they move together.

public.prompt: QuickShip finds that distance_km and delivery_minutes have a strong positive correlation (0.82). A colleague says this proves distance is the direct cause of longer delivery times. What is the best response?

options.text: A confounding variable — such as traffic zone, which correlates with both distance and delivery time — could produce this association without distance being the direct cause
The colleague is right: a correlation of 0.82 is strong enough to confirm causation
The correlation is too weak to draw any conclusion
The association must run the other way: longer delivery times cause greater distances

opt_confound.message: Correct. A confounding variable correlated with both distance and delivery time could produce the observed association without distance being the direct cause.

opt_agree.message: Not quite. No matter how strong a correlation is, it cannot by itself confirm causation. A confounding variable could explain the association.

opt_weak.message: Not quite. A correlation of 0.82 is strong, not weak. The issue is not the strength but the fact that correlation alone cannot establish causation.

opt_reverse.message: Not quite. Reversing the direction is one possibility, but the key point is that a confounding variable could also explain the association — correlation alone cannot determine the causal direction.

correct.message: Right. A strong correlation is consistent with causation but does not prove it — a confounding variable could be responsible.

incorrect.message: Remember: a confounding variable is one that correlates with both variables being studied, producing an association that is not a direct link.

hints: Could a third variable — one correlated with both distance and delivery time — explain the association?
A confounding variable is correlated with both of the variables being studied.

public.intro: Use the correlation matrix to rank the three variable pairs by the strength of their linear relationship.

tasks.prompt: Select the cell showing the pair with the strongest linear relationship (highest absolute value, excluding the diagonal).
Select the cell showing the pair with the middle-ranked strength (excluding the diagonal).
Select the cell showing the pair with the weakest linear relationship (lowest absolute value, excluding the diagonal).

task_strongest_magnitude.correct: Correct. |0.82| = 0.82 is the largest absolute value — distance_km and delivery_minutes have the strongest relationship.
task_strongest_magnitude.incorrect: Not quite. Take the absolute value of each off-diagonal cell and pick the largest.

task_middle_magnitude.correct: Correct. |-0.41| = 0.41 is the middle value — package_weight_kg and delivery_minutes have a moderate relationship.
task_middle_magnitude.incorrect: Not quite. After finding the strongest and weakest, the remaining pair is the middle-ranked one.

task_weakest_magnitude.correct: Correct. |-0.38| = 0.38 is the smallest absolute value — distance_km and package_weight_kg have the weakest relationship.
task_weakest_magnitude.incorrect: Not quite. Take the absolute value of each off-diagonal cell and pick the smallest.

correct.message: Excellent. You ranked all three pairs correctly by absolute value, ignoring the sign.

incorrect.message: Strength is judged by absolute value — ignore the sign and compare the magnitudes.

hints: Ignore the sign. Take the absolute value of each off-diagonal cell to compare strengths.
The diagonal (1.0) is each variable with itself — skip those cells.

public.prompt: A report states: 'Priority deliveries cause faster delivery times.' The only evidence is observational data showing priority orders tend to have shorter delivery times. Which restatement is correct?

options.text: Priority orders are associated with shorter delivery times, though we cannot confirm from this data that priority status causes the difference
The original statement is fine — observational data is sufficient to claim causation
The finding should be dropped entirely because observational data proves nothing
The finding should be stated only as a hypothesis with no supporting evidence

opt_assoc.message: Correct. When only observational data supports a finding, it should be restated as an association rather than a causal claim.

opt_causal_ok.message: Not quite. Observational data alone cannot establish causation. The finding should be restated as an association or a hypothesis to check later.

opt_no_rel.message: Not quite. The finding is still useful — it just needs to be restated as an association rather than a causal claim. Observational findings are valid evidence of association.

opt_hypothesis_only.message: Not quite. The observational data does support the association — it just cannot confirm causation. The correct restatement acknowledges the association while flagging the causal claim.

correct.message: Right. Observational data supports an association, not a causal claim. Restate the finding accordingly.

incorrect.message: When only observational data is available, restate the finding as an association or a hypothesis to check later — not as a causal claim.

hints: What kind of data supports this finding — experimental or observational?
Observational data can show that two things tend to occur together, but cannot prove one causes the other.

public.intro: The table shows QuickShip orders with their priority flag and delivery time. A colleague claims: 'Selecting priority causes faster delivery.' Use the data to evaluate this claim.

tasks.prompt: Select a row where priority is true and delivery_minutes is among the shortest in the dataset — evidence the two variables are associated.
Select a row where priority is true but delivery_minutes is not especially short — evidence that priority alone does not guarantee fast delivery.

task_priority_true_fast.correct: Correct. ORD-113 is a priority order with a delivery time of 17 minutes — one of the shortest in the dataset.
task_priority_true_fast.incorrect: Look for a row where priority is true and delivery_minutes is very low (17 or 18 minutes).

task_priority_true_slow.correct: Correct. ORD-103 is a priority order with a delivery time of 36 minutes — not especially fast. This shows priority is associated with, but does not guarantee, faster delivery.
task_priority_true_slow.incorrect: Look for a row where priority is true but delivery_minutes is 36 or higher.

correct.message: Well done. The data shows an association between priority and delivery time, but the variation in priority rows shows it is not a guaranteed causal link.

incorrect.message: Look for rows where priority is true. Do all of them have short delivery times? That variation is the key evidence against a simple causal claim.

hints: Find rows where priority is true. Are all their delivery times short?
If priority caused faster delivery in every case, all priority rows would have short delivery times.

public.prompt: Which set of attributes best describes the Customer entity in the QuickShip database?

options.text: customer_id, name, city
order_id, delivery_minutes, priority
customer_id, order_id, delivery_minutes
name only

opt_correct.message: Correct. customer_id, name, and city are all attributes that describe a customer — they belong to the Customer entity.

opt_order_attrs.message: Not quite. order_id, delivery_minutes, and priority describe an order, not a customer. Each entity is described by attributes that belong to that specific real-world thing.

opt_mixed.message: Not quite. order_id and delivery_minutes are attributes of the Order entity, not the Customer entity. Attributes should describe the same real-world thing.

opt_too_few.message: Not quite. While name is one attribute of a customer, an entity is described by a set of attributes — customer_id and city also describe a customer.

correct.message: Right. Each entity is described by the set of attributes that belong to that real-world thing.

incorrect.message: Think about which attributes describe a customer specifically — not an order or any other entity.

hints: Attributes describe the entity they belong to. Which of these values tell you something about a customer?
An entity's attributes are the columns in its table. What columns would you expect in a Customers table?

public.prompt: QuickShip tracks customers, the orders they place, and the products in each order. Each customer has a name and a city; each order has a delivery time; each product has a name. Classify each item below as either an Entity (a real-world thing that gets its own table) or an Attribute (a property that describes an entity).

items.text: Customer
Order
Product
delivery_minutes
city

item_customer.message: Correct. Customer is an entity — a real-world thing with independent existence that gets its own table.

item_order.message: Correct. Order is an entity — each order is a distinct real-world event that gets its own table.

item_product.message: Correct. Product is an entity — a real-world thing (physical or conceptual) that gets its own table.

item_delivery_minutes.message: Correct. delivery_minutes is an attribute — it describes an order, not a real-world thing that gets its own table.

item_city.message: Correct. city is an attribute — it describes a customer, not a real-world thing that gets its own table.

correct.message: Well done. You correctly separated the real-world things (entities) from the properties that describe them (attributes).

incorrect.message: An entity is a real-world thing with independent existence that gets its own table. An attribute is a property that describes an entity.

hints: Ask: does this thing exist independently in the real world, or does it describe something else?
Entities become tables; attributes become columns in those tables.

public.prompt: A new row is inserted into the customers table with a NULL value in the customer_id column. What does entity integrity say about this?

options.text: This violates entity integrity — the primary key must never be null
This is acceptable — null means the value is unknown, which is allowed in a primary key
This is acceptable as long as no other row has the same null value
It depends on whether the table has other non-null columns

opt_violates.message: Correct. Entity integrity requires that every table have a primary key and that neither the primary key nor any part of it contain null values.

opt_ok_null.message: Not quite. Entity integrity explicitly forbids null values in the primary key. A null primary key means the row cannot be uniquely identified.

opt_ok_if_unique.message: Not quite. Null values are not comparable — two null values are not considered equal or unequal. Entity integrity forbids null in the primary key regardless of other rows.

opt_depends.message: Not quite. Entity integrity applies to the primary key column specifically. A null primary key always violates entity integrity, regardless of other columns.

correct.message: Right. Entity integrity requires the primary key to be both unique and never null.

incorrect.message: Entity integrity has two requirements: the primary key must be unique, and it must never contain null values.

hints: What are the two requirements entity integrity places on a primary key?
If a primary key is null, can you uniquely identify that row?

public.intro: The table shows four candidate columns for the primary key of the customers table. Examine each column's values to decide which can serve as the primary key.

tasks.prompt: Select the column that can serve as the primary key — its values are unique and never null.
Select the cell that shows why the phone column cannot be the primary key.
Select a cell that shows why the name column cannot be the primary key (a duplicate value).

task_valid_pk_column.correct: Correct. customer_id has unique values and no nulls — it satisfies both requirements for a primary key.
task_valid_pk_column.incorrect: Check each column: does it have unique values in every row? Does it have any null values? Only one column passes both tests.

task_null_fail.correct: Correct. Customer 4 has a null phone value. A primary key must never be null, so phone cannot serve as the primary key.
task_null_fail.incorrect: Look for the row where the phone column is empty (null). That null value is why phone fails as a primary key.

task_duplicate_fail.correct: Correct. Customer 5 shares the name 'Amara Okafor' with customer 1. A primary key must be unique, so name cannot serve as the primary key.
task_duplicate_fail.incorrect: Look for a name value that appears more than once. That duplicate is why name fails as a primary key.

correct.message: Well done. You identified the valid primary key and spotted the exact values that disqualify the other candidates.

incorrect.message: A valid primary key must have unique values in every row and no null values. Check each column against both requirements.

hints: Scan each column for repeated values or blank (null) cells.
A primary key fails if any value is null or if any value appears more than once.

public.prompt: An orders row has customer_id = 99, but no row in the customers table has customer_id = 99. What is this row called, and what rule does it break?

options.text: An orphan record — it breaks referential integrity because the foreign key value has no matching primary key in the referenced table
A valid row — a null or unmatched foreign key is always acceptable
A duplicate record — it breaks the uniqueness requirement of the primary key
An entity integrity violation — the primary key of the orders table is null

opt_orphan.message: Correct. A row whose foreign key value is not found in the referenced table is called an orphan record, and referential integrity is what prevents these.

opt_null_ok.message: Not quite. A null foreign key is acceptable, but a non-null foreign key that has no matching primary key in the referenced table is not. That creates an orphan record and breaks referential integrity.

opt_duplicate.message: Not quite. This is not a duplicate-row issue. The problem is that the foreign key value (99) does not match any primary key in the customers table — that is an orphan record violating referential integrity.

opt_entity.message: Not quite. Entity integrity is about the primary key being non-null. The issue here is the foreign key value (99) having no match in the referenced table — that is a referential integrity violation.

correct.message: Right. A non-null foreign key that has no matching primary key in the referenced table creates an orphan record and breaks referential integrity.

incorrect.message: Remember: referential integrity requires that a non-null foreign key value must match an existing primary key in the referenced table.

hints: What is the term for a row whose foreign key value has no matching row in the referenced table?
A null foreign key is fine. A non-null foreign key with no match is the problem.

public.intro: The orders table has been modified so that one row references a customer that does not exist in the customers table. Use the table to answer the tasks below.

tasks.prompt: Select the column in the orders table that is the foreign key referencing the customers table.
Select the row that creates an orphan record — its foreign key value has no matching primary key in the customers table.
Select the specific cell containing the foreign key value that breaks referential integrity.

task_fk_column.correct: Correct. customer_id in the orders table is the foreign key — its values must match a customer_id in the customers table.
task_fk_column.incorrect: The foreign key is the column whose values reference the primary key of another table. Which column in orders points to the customers table?

task_orphan_row.correct: Correct. Order 107 has customer_id = 99, which does not exist in the customers table — making it an orphan record.
task_orphan_row.incorrect: Check each row's customer_id value. Which one does not appear in the customers table (valid customer_ids are 1–5)?

task_orphan_cell.correct: Correct. The value 99 in the customer_id column of order 107 has no matching row in the customers table, breaking referential integrity.
task_orphan_cell.incorrect: Find the row with the unmatched customer_id and select the cell in the customer_id column for that row.

correct.message: Excellent. You identified the foreign key column and pinpointed the exact cell that breaks referential integrity.

incorrect.message: The foreign key column links orders to customers. An orphan record has a foreign key value that matches no primary key in the referenced table.

hints: The foreign key is the column that references another table's primary key. Which column in orders does that?
Valid customer_ids in the customers table are 1 through 5. Which order row has a customer_id outside that range?

public.prompt: In the QuickShip database, one customer can place many orders. Where should the foreign key (customer_id) be placed?

options.text: In the orders table — the many side holds the foreign key
In the customers table — the one side holds the foreign key
In both tables — each side needs a copy of the foreign key
In neither table — a separate linking table is always required

opt_orders.message: Correct. In a one-to-many relationship, the foreign key is placed in the table on the many side — here, the orders table.

opt_customers.message: Not quite. Placing the foreign key in the customers table would require storing multiple order IDs in one customer row, which is not how relational tables work. The foreign key goes in the orders table (the many side).

opt_both.message: Not quite. Only the many side needs the foreign key. Placing it in both tables would create redundancy and inconsistency.

opt_neither.message: Not quite. A separate junction table is needed for many-to-many relationships, not one-to-many. In a 1:M relationship, the foreign key goes directly in the many-side table.

correct.message: Right. The foreign key always goes in the many-side table — here, orders holds customer_id to reference the customers table.

incorrect.message: In a one-to-many relationship, the many side holds the foreign key. Think about which table has multiple rows per entity on the other side.

hints: Which table has multiple rows for a single customer? That is the many side.
The many side holds the foreign key because each row on the many side references exactly one row on the one side.

public.intro: The orders table is shown below. Customer 1 (Amara Okafor) has placed orders 101 and 103; customer 2 (Emeka Nwosu) has placed orders 102 and 106. Use the table to answer the tasks.

tasks.prompt: Select a row that shows the same customer_id appearing more than once — evidence that orders is the many side of the relationship.
Select the column in the orders table that is the foreign key linking each order to its customer.

task_many_side_evidence.correct: Correct. Order 103 also has customer_id = 1, showing that customer 1 has multiple orders — confirming orders is the many side.
task_many_side_evidence.incorrect: Look for a customer_id value that appears in more than one row. That repetition shows orders is the many side.

task_fk_in_orders.correct: Correct. customer_id in the orders table is the foreign key — it references the primary key of the customers table and is placed on the many side.
task_fk_in_orders.incorrect: The foreign key is the column that references another table's primary key. Which column in orders points to the customers table?

correct.message: Well done. You identified the many side (orders) and the foreign key column (customer_id) that links each order to its customer.

incorrect.message: The many side is the table where the same value from the other table appears in multiple rows. The foreign key is the column that creates that link.

hints: Look for a customer_id value that appears in more than one row in the orders table.
The foreign key is in the orders table because each order belongs to exactly one customer, but one customer can have many orders.

public.prompt: A single orders table stores customer_id, customer_name, customer_city, and delivery_minutes on every row. A customer with five orders has their name and city repeated five times. Which change removes that redundancy?

options.text: Move customer_name and customer_city into a separate customers table, linked back by customer_id
Add an index on customer_name to speed up lookups
Replace repeated customer_name values with NULL after the first row
Sort the table by customer_id so repeated rows are grouped together

opt_split.message: Correct. Moving the repeating data into a separate table and linking it by key is exactly how normalization removes redundancy — each customer's name and city is stored once.

opt_index.message: Not quite. An index speeds up queries but does not remove the repeated data; the name and city are still stored five times.

opt_null.message: Not quite. Replacing repeated values with NULL would break the data — you would lose the customer's name and city for most orders. Normalization moves the data to a separate table, not removes it.

opt_sort.message: Not quite. Sorting groups the repeated rows visually but does not remove the redundancy — the name and city are still stored five times, and an update anomaly is still possible.

correct.message: Exactly right. Splitting the repeating data into a separate table and linking by key is the normalization move that removes redundancy.

incorrect.message: Remember: normalization removes redundancy by moving repeating data into a new table linked by a key column.

hints: Think about what 'removing redundancy' means — the data should be stored only once.
Which option actually changes where the data lives, rather than just changing how it looks or how fast it can be found?

public.instructions: The table below shows a customers table where a data entry error has introduced a duplicate row. Flag the cell that reveals the redundancy problem — the repeated customer_id that would cause an update anomaly if the customer's details changed.

issues.explanation: customer_id 1 appears twice. This duplicate row means that if Amara Okafor's city changes, both rows must be updated — missing one creates an update anomaly where the same customer appears to live in two different cities.

decoys.message: customer_id 2 (Emeka Nwosu) appears only once — no redundancy here.
customer_id 3 (Fatima Bello) appears only once — no redundancy here.

grading.wrong_category_message: You found the duplicate row, but check the category. A repeated customer_id is a redundancy problem — it creates an update anomaly risk, not a clean record.
grading.completion_message: Well done. You identified the duplicate row for customer_id 1. Storing the same customer twice means any update to their details must be applied to both rows — missing one leaves inconsistent data.

correct.message: Correct. The duplicate row for customer_id 1 is the redundancy problem. If the customer's city changes, both rows must be updated — missing one creates an update anomaly.

incorrect.message: Look for a customer_id that appears more than once. That repeated row is the redundancy that normalization removes.

hints: Scan the customer_id column for any value that appears more than once.
A redundant row means the same customer's details are stored twice — what happens if their city changes?

public.prompt: A junction table called enrollments resolves a many-to-many relationship between students and courses. Which columns must it contain, and what forms its primary key?

options.text: It must contain student_id and course_id as foreign keys; the pair (student_id, course_id) forms the primary key
It must contain only student_id as a foreign key; course_id is optional
It must contain student_id and course_id, but needs a separate enrollment_id as its primary key
It must contain student_name and course_name so the data is self-contained

opt_correct.message: Correct. The junction table must contain the primary keys of both original tables as foreign keys, and the combination of those two foreign keys forms the primary key of the junction table.

opt_one_fk.message: Not quite. A junction table must contain the primary keys of both original tables as foreign keys — both student_id and course_id are required to record which student is enrolled in which course.

opt_new_pk.message: Not quite. While a separate surrogate key is sometimes added, the combination of the two foreign keys (student_id, course_id) is what makes the primary key of the junction table — that pair is unique because the same student won't enrol in the same course twice.

opt_no_fk.message: Not quite. Storing names instead of keys reintroduces redundancy and breaks the relational link. The junction table must contain the primary keys of both original tables as foreign keys.

correct.message: Exactly right. The junction table holds the primary keys of both original tables as foreign keys, and their combination is the primary key.

incorrect.message: Remember: the junction table must contain the primary keys of both original tables as foreign keys, and those two keys together form the junction table's primary key.

hints: What two pieces of information does the junction table need to record a single enrollment?
The primary key of the junction table must uniquely identify each pairing — what combination of columns achieves that?

task_fk_order.correct: Correct. order_id is a foreign key referencing orders.order_id — it links each row back to the order it belongs to.
task_fk_order.incorrect: Not quite. Look for the column that references the orders table by storing the order's primary key.

task_fk_product.incorrect: Not quite. Look for the column that references the products table by storing the product's primary key.

task_pk_pair_order.correct: Correct. order_id 101 is the first half of the composite primary key for this pairing.
task_pk_pair_order.incorrect: Not quite. Select the order_id value in the row where order 101 is paired with product 10 (the rice bag).

task_pk_pair_product.correct: Correct. product_id 10 completes the composite primary key (101, 10) — this pair is unique because the same order won't list the same product twice.
task_pk_pair_product.incorrect: Not quite. Select the product_id value in the row where order 101 is paired with product 10 (the rice bag).

correct.message: Well done. You identified both foreign key columns and the composite primary key pair — the two foreign keys together uniquely identify each order/product pairing.

incorrect.message: Review the junction table structure. Each column is a foreign key to one of the original tables, and together they form the composite primary key.

hints: Each column in the junction table is a foreign key to one of the two original tables — which table does each column reference?
The composite primary key is the pair of foreign keys — find the row where order 101 is paired with product 10.

public.prompt: A relationship line between Customer and Order has a three-pronged symbol on the Order side and a one-and-only-one symbol on the Customer side. What does this mean?

options.text: Each customer must have exactly one order, and each order can belong to many customers
Each order must be linked to exactly one customer (mandatory), and one customer can be linked to many orders
Many customers can be linked to many orders
A customer may have zero or one order, and each order belongs to exactly one customer

opt_correct.message: Correct. The one-and-only-one symbol on the Customer side means each order must be linked to exactly one customer (mandatory). The three-pronged symbol on the Order side means one customer can be linked to many orders — a one-to-many relationship.

opt_one_to_many.message: Not quite. The three-pronged symbol is on the Order side, meaning 'many orders' per customer — not 'many customers' per order. The one-and-only-one symbol on the Customer side means each order belongs to exactly one customer.

opt_many_to_many.message: Not quite. A many-to-many relationship would require three-pronged symbols on both sides. Here only the Order side has the three-pronged symbol, making this a one-to-many relationship.

opt_optional.message: Not quite. A 'zero or one' symbol would show a zero and a one together. The one-and-only-one symbol means mandatory — exactly one customer per order, not zero or one.

correct.message: Correct. The three-pronged symbol means 'many' on the Order side; the one-and-only-one symbol means each order must belong to exactly one customer.

incorrect.message: Remember: a three-pronged symbol means 'many'; a one-and-only-one symbol means that side is mandatory (exactly one).

hints: Which side of the line has the three-pronged symbol? That side is the 'many' side.
The one-and-only-one symbol means that side is mandatory — every order must be linked to exactly one customer.

public.prompt: The QuickShip ER diagram contains four entity boxes (Customer, Order, Product, Order_Item), attribute ovals, underlined primary keys, and relationship lines. Classify each element below as it would appear in the diagram.

buckets.label: Not an ERD element (data value, not structure)

items.text: Customer — the rectangle labelled 'Customer'
Order — the rectangle labelled 'Order'
customer_id — the oval attached to Customer, with its name underlined
city — the oval attached to Customer, name not underlined
The line between Customer and Order (three-pronged symbol on the Order side)
The line between Order and Product (three-pronged symbols on both sides, resolved via Order_Item)
Order_Item — the rectangle labelled 'Order_Item'
customer_id = 1 — the integer value stored in the first row of the customers table

item_customer_box.message: Correct. In an ERD, an entity type is represented by its name inside a rectangle — Customer is an entity box.

item_order_box.message: Correct. Order is an entity type, drawn as a rectangle labelled 'Order'.

item_customer_id_oval.message: Correct. customer_id is the primary key attribute of Customer — it is shown as an oval with its name underlined.

item_city_oval.message: Correct. city is a regular attribute of Customer — shown as an oval without underlining, since it is not the primary key.

item_customer_order_line.message: Correct. The three-pronged symbol on the Order side means 'many orders per customer' — a one-to-many relationship line.

item_order_product_line.message: Correct. Three-pronged symbols on both sides indicate a many-to-many relationship between Order and Product (resolved in the schema by the Order_Item junction table).

item_order_item_box.message: Correct. Order_Item is an entity type (the junction/composite entity), drawn as a rectangle in the ERD.

item_trap_customer_id_number.message: Correct. This is a data value (the integer 1 stored in a row), not an ERD element. In an ERD, customer_id appears as an underlined oval (a primary key attribute), not as a row value. The ERD shows structure, not data.

correct.message: Excellent. You correctly identified entities, attributes, primary keys, and relationship types — and recognised that a data value is not an ERD element.

incorrect.message: Review the ERD notation: rectangles are entities, ovals are attributes, underlined ovals are primary keys, and lines with cardinality markings show relationships.

hints: In an ERD, shapes matter: rectangles are entities, ovals are attributes. Is the item a shape in the diagram or a value in a table row?
For relationship lines, count the prongs: one prong on each side means one-to-one; three prongs on one side means one-to-many; three prongs on both sides means many-to-many.

public.prompt: Average Kano delivery times rose from 21.0 to 22.5 minutes between Month 1 and Month 2. Which option best follows the 'because we found X, we recommend Y' pattern?

options.text: Because average Kano delivery times rose from 21.0 to 22.5 minutes, we recommend adding a courier to the Kano route.
We recommend adding a courier to the Kano route to improve performance.
Because delivery times have been increasing, we recommend reviewing operations.
We should add a courier to the Kano route because that is what the operations manager wants.

opt_correct.message: Correct. This recommendation names the specific finding (21.0 to 22.5 minutes) and connects it directly to a concrete action (adding a courier) — exactly the 'because X, we recommend Y' pattern.

opt_no_finding.message: Not quite. This recommendation states an action but gives no data finding to justify it. A data-driven recommendation must cite the specific finding that supports the action.

opt_vague.message: Not quite. 'Delivery times have been increasing' is too vague — it does not cite the specific numbers. A data-driven recommendation names the precise finding.

opt_reversed.message: Not quite. This justifies the recommendation by what the manager wants, not by a data finding. The 'because X' part must be a data result, not a stakeholder preference.

correct.message: Correct. A data-driven recommendation names the specific finding and connects it to a concrete action.

incorrect.message: Remember: the recommendation must cite the specific data finding ('because we found X') and connect it to a concrete action ('we recommend Y').

hints: Which option actually names a specific number from the data as the reason for the recommendation?
The 'because' clause must be a data result — a specific finding, not a general observation or a stakeholder preference.

public.intro: The table shows average delivery times and order volumes for three cities across two months. Select the cells that provide the strongest data justification for a recommendation to add a courier to the Lagos route.

tasks.prompt: Select the cell showing Lagos's average delivery time in Month 1 — the baseline before the increase.
Select the cell showing Lagos's average delivery time in Month 2 — the value that reveals the problem.

task_baseline_value.correct: Correct. 22.0 minutes is the Lagos baseline in Month 1 — the starting point that makes the Month 2 increase meaningful.
task_baseline_value.incorrect: Not quite. Look for the Lagos row in Month 1 and select the average delivery time — that is the baseline before the increase.

task_current_value.correct: Correct. 30.0 minutes in Month 2 is the finding that justifies the recommendation — the rise from 22.0 to 30.0 minutes is the 'because X' in 'because we found X, we recommend Y'.
task_current_value.incorrect: Not quite. Look for the Lagos row in Month 2 and select the average delivery time — that is the value that reveals the problem.

correct.message: Well done. The rise from 22.0 to 30.0 minutes in Lagos is the specific finding that justifies a recommendation — 'because average Lagos delivery times rose from 22.0 to 30.0 minutes, we recommend adding a courier to the Lagos route.'

incorrect.message: Look for the Lagos rows and select the average delivery time values that show the change between months.

hints: A data-driven recommendation needs a specific 'before' and 'after' value — which city shows the largest change?
Find the Lagos rows and compare the average delivery times across the two months.

public.prompt: Which word best replaces 'utilise' in the sentence: 'We should utilise the new courier route to reduce delivery times'?

options.text: use
employ
leverage
implement

opt_use.message: Correct. 'Use' is the short, everyday word that replaces the formal 'utilise' — plain language prefers the simpler equivalent.

opt_employ.message: Not quite. 'Employ' is also a formal word — it is no simpler than 'utilise'. Plain language calls for the shortest, most everyday word: 'use'.

opt_leverage.message: Not quite. 'Leverage' is a buzzword that is often vague and can be misinterpreted. Plain language avoids jargon and buzzwords; 'use' is the clear, simple choice.

opt_implement.message: Not quite. 'Implement' is a formal word that is longer and less everyday than 'use'. Plain language prefers the short, simple equivalent.

correct.message: Correct. 'Use' is the short, everyday word that replaces the formal 'utilise' — exactly the kind of substitution plain language calls for.

incorrect.message: Remember: plain language replaces formal or long words with short, everyday equivalents. 'Utilise' → 'use' is a classic example.

hints: Which of the options is the shortest, most everyday word for the same action?
Plain language avoids formal words like 'utilise', 'employ', and buzzwords like 'leverage' — which option is the simplest?

public.prompt: Each sentence below is a plain-language rewrite of a technical result. Classify each rewrite by which plain-language rule it applies: Rule 1 — specialist terms are glossed on first use; Rule 2 — formal or long words are replaced with simpler equivalents.

buckets.label: Rule 1 only — specialist term glossed in plain English
Rule 2 only — formal word replaced with a simpler one

items.text: The average (mean) Lagos delivery time rose from 22 to 30 minutes.
Lagos delivery times got worse this month.
The average (mean) delivery time — how long each order takes from dispatch to doorstep — rose by 8 minutes, so we recommend adding a courier.
Delivery time performance exhibited negative variance this period.

item_gloss_only.message: Correct. 'The average (mean)' glosses the specialist term 'mean' in plain English on first use — Rule 1. No formal words are replaced here, so only Rule 1 applies.

item_replace_only.message: Correct. 'Got worse' replaces the formal phrase 'exhibited negative variance' with a short, everyday equivalent — Rule 2. No specialist term is glossed, so only Rule 2 applies.

item_both.message: Correct. 'The average (mean)' glosses the specialist term (Rule 1), and the sentence replaces formal alternatives with plain words like 'rose' instead of 'increased' and 'recommend' instead of 'advise' (Rule 2). Both rules are applied.

item_trap.message: This sentence applies neither rule. 'Exhibited' is a formal word that should be replaced with 'showed' or 'got worse' (Rule 2 not applied), and 'negative variance' is jargon that is not glossed (Rule 1 not applied). This is the kind of technical sentence that needs to be rewritten.

correct.message: Well done. You correctly identified which plain-language rule each rewrite applies — and spotted the sentence that applies neither rule.

incorrect.message: Review the two rules: Rule 1 glosses specialist terms on first use; Rule 2 replaces formal or long words with simpler equivalents. Which rule does each rewrite apply?

hints: Look for parenthetical glosses like '(mean)' — that is Rule 1 in action. Look for short, everyday words replacing formal ones — that is Rule 2.
One sentence applies neither rule — it still uses formal language and unexplained jargon. Which one is it?

public.prompt: An operations manager prefers detail-oriented presentations. Which approach best fits this audience?

options.text: Start with the specifics of the analysis, then present next steps
Start with the high-level recommendation only
Alternate between high-level and detailed sections
Use only charts and visuals without text explanation

opt_detail_first.message: Correct. Technical or detail-oriented people like operations managers prefer to understand the specifics of an analysis first before considering next steps.

opt_high_level.message: Not quite. Operations managers are detail-oriented and typically want to understand the specifics of the analysis, not just a high-level recommendation.

opt_mixed.message: Not quite. For detail-oriented audiences, it's better to present the analysis systematically, starting with specifics, rather than alternating between levels.

opt_visual_only.message: Not quite. While visuals are helpful, detail-oriented audiences also want text explanations of the methodology and findings.

correct.message: Right. Tailoring to the audience means adjusting both the depth of detail and the order in which you present it.

incorrect.message: Remember: executives want the high-level arc first; detail-oriented audiences want to understand the specifics before considering recommendations.

hints: Think about whether each audience type prefers detail-first or recommendation-first.
Technical audiences typically want to understand the analysis before hearing recommendations.

public.prompt: Two versions of the Lagos finding are shown. Classify each version by its intended audience and identify the signal that reveals the target audience.

items.text: Version A: 'We recommend adding a second Lagos hub. Analysis shows 40% of deliveries exceed target time, with the longest delays in the eastern districts. A second hub would cut average delivery time by 18 minutes.'

Version B: 'Lagos delivery data shows 40% of orders exceed the 60-minute target. Eastern districts average 78 minutes (18 minutes over target). Peak delay hours are 2–5 PM. A second hub in the eastern zone would reduce average delivery time to 42 minutes, bringing 85% of deliveries within target.'

correct.message: Exactly right. Version A starts with the recommendation and provides high-level context — suited for an executive. Version B leads with detailed analysis and specifics — suited for an operations manager.

incorrect.message: Look at the order and density of information. Which version starts with the recommendation? Which version includes day-by-day breakdowns and specific numbers?

hints: Version A starts with 'We recommend' — what does that signal about the intended audience?
Version B includes specific time breakdowns and percentages — what type of audience prefers that level of detail?

public.prompt: Which addition to the Lagos report best addresses a likely question from the operations manager?

options.text: A detailed cost breakdown showing the investment required for a second hub
A comparison of QuickShip's delivery times to competitor benchmarks
A timeline showing how the second hub would be implemented
A note explaining how the delivery-time data was collected and validated

opt_cost_breakdown.message: Not the best fit. While cost matters, an operations manager is more likely to ask about the data quality and methodology behind the analysis before considering implementation costs.

opt_competitor.message: Not the best fit. Competitor benchmarks might be useful context, but an operations manager is more likely to first ask about the reliability of the data driving the recommendation.

opt_implementation.message: Not the best fit. Implementation details matter, but a detail-oriented operations manager will first want to understand how the data was collected and whether it is trustworthy.

opt_data_quality.message: Correct. Being tailored to the audience means anticipating their questions. A detail-oriented operations manager will likely ask about data quality and methodology before accepting the recommendation.

correct.message: Right. Detail-oriented audiences want to understand the specifics of how the analysis was done, including data quality and methodology.

incorrect.message: Think about what a detail-oriented operations manager would want to know first. They typically scrutinize the data and methodology before considering recommendations.

hints: What would a detail-oriented audience want to verify before trusting the recommendation?
Operations managers often ask about data quality and how the analysis was conducted.

public.prompt: For a detail-oriented audience, what is the benefit of presenting findings before making a request?

options.text: It builds trust by showing the data and analysis before asking for action
It saves time by getting straight to the recommendation
It avoids questions by providing all the details upfront
It simplifies the message by reducing the amount of information

opt_builds_trust.message: Correct. Technical or detail-oriented people prefer to understand the specifics of an analysis first, so they are prepared to take in ideas about next steps. This builds trust and credibility.

opt_saves_time.message: Not quite. For detail-oriented audiences, presenting findings first actually takes more time initially, but it builds the foundation they need to accept the recommendation.

opt_avoids_questions.message: Not quite. The goal is not to avoid questions but to prepare the audience so they can engage meaningfully with the recommendation. Detail-oriented audiences will still ask questions.

opt_simplifies.message: Not quite. Presenting findings first actually adds more information, not less. The benefit is that it prepares detail-oriented audiences to accept the recommendation.

correct.message: Exactly. Detail-oriented audiences want to understand the specifics first so they are prepared to consider next steps. This sequence builds trust.

incorrect.message: Remember: detail-oriented audiences prefer to understand the analysis before hearing recommendations. This prepares them to accept the request.

hints: Think about what detail-oriented audiences need before they can accept a recommendation.
Presenting findings first helps the audience feel prepared and builds credibility.

public.prompt: For each report section below, classify whether it anticipates a likely stakeholder question or is purely descriptive.

items.text: Data Quality: Delivery times were recorded automatically by the GPS tracking system. We validated 95% of records against driver logs and found no systematic errors.
Finding: 40% of Lagos deliveries exceed the 60-minute target, with eastern districts averaging 78 minutes.
Alternative Explanations: We considered whether traffic patterns or seasonal effects could explain the delays. Analysis shows the pattern is consistent across seasons and time of day.
Recommendation: Add a second hub in the eastern zone to reduce average delivery time to 42 minutes.

correct.message: Excellent. You identified the sections that anticipate stakeholder questions: data quality (how was this measured?), alternative explanations (what else could explain this?), and implementation risks (what could go wrong?).

incorrect.message: Look for sections that address questions a stakeholder might ask: How was the data collected? What else could explain the pattern? What are the risks?

hints: Stakeholders often ask about data quality and methodology.
Detail-oriented audiences want to know about alternative explanations and potential risks.

public.prompt: A scatterplot of distance_km vs delivery_minutes is shown. Is this chart primarily exploratory or communicative?

options.text: Exploratory — scatterplots are often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it
Communicative — scatterplots are designed to present findings to stakeholders
Both — scatterplots work equally well for exploration and communication
Neither — scatterplots are only used for statistical modeling

opt_exploratory.message: Correct. A scatterplot is often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it. For stakeholder communication, you would typically choose a simpler chart type.

opt_communicative.message: Not quite. Scatterplots are powerful for exploration, but they are often too complex for stakeholder communication. Simpler chart types like bar charts or line graphs are usually better for presenting findings.

opt_both.message: Not quite. While scatterplots can be used for both purposes, they are primarily exploratory tools. For communication, simpler chart types are usually more effective.

opt_neither.message: Not quite. Scatterplots are used for exploration and can support modeling, but their primary role is to help analysts understand relationships in the data.

correct.message: Right. Scatterplots are exploratory tools. For stakeholder communication, choose simpler chart types that match your point.

incorrect.message: Remember: scatterplots are often used to understand data rather than to communicate with it. For stakeholders, simpler charts are usually better.

hints: Think about whether a scatterplot is easy for a non-technical audience to interpret.
Scatterplots show many individual data points — is that level of detail needed for communication?

public.prompt: For each stakeholder point below, classify the best chart type from the set: bar chart, line graph, pie chart, boxplot.

items.text: Compare average delivery times across five cities
Show how delivery times changed month by month over the past year
Show that Lagos accounts for 35% of total delivery volume
Compare the distribution of delivery times across three regions for a technical audience

correct.message: Excellent. You matched each point to the right chart type: bar chart for categorical comparison, line graph for trends over time, pie chart for part-to-whole, and boxplot for distribution comparison with a technical audience.

incorrect.message: Think about what each chart type does best. Bar charts compare categories, line graphs show change over time, pie charts show part-to-whole, and boxplots compare distributions.

hints: Bar charts are best for comparing values across categories.
Line graphs show how something changes over time.
Pie charts express part-to-whole relationships.
Boxplots compare distributions but may be unfamiliar to non-technical audiences.

public.prompt: Which elements should be removed from a bar chart prepared for a non-technical operations manager?

options.text: Gridlines and the chart border, since they add no informative value
Axis labels, since the bars speak for themselves
All data labels, since they clutter the chart
Nothing — all elements are necessary for clarity

opt_gridlines_border.message: Correct. Gridlines can be deleted if precise values are not critical, and a chart's border can be removed since it adds no informative value. White space is enough to separate the chart from surrounding content.

opt_axis_labels.message: Not quite. Axis labels are essential for understanding what the chart shows. Removing them would make the chart confusing, not simpler.

opt_data_labels.message: Not quite. Data labels should be used sparingly, but they are helpful where exact values matter. The goal is to remove elements that add no informative value, not all labels.

opt_nothing.message: Not quite. Many chart elements add clutter without adding information. Gridlines and borders can often be removed to let the audience focus on the data.

correct.message: Right. Reducing clutter lets the audience use their attention to decide what actions might be taken, rather than decoding the chart.

incorrect.message: Think about which elements add informative value and which are just decoration. Gridlines and borders often fall into the decoration category.

hints: Which elements help the audience understand the data, and which are just visual decoration?
Gridlines and borders can often be removed without losing clarity.

public.prompt: What does removing a chart's border achieve?

options.text: It reduces clutter; white space is enough to separate the chart from surrounding content
It makes the chart look more modern and professional
It makes the chart area larger so more data can be shown
Nothing — borders are necessary to define the chart boundaries

opt_white_space.message: Correct. A chart's border can be removed since it is not adding informative value; white space is enough to separate the chart from surrounding content.

opt_modern.message: Not quite. While removing borders may look modern, the real benefit is reducing clutter. The border adds no informative value, and white space is sufficient for separation.

opt_larger.message: Not quite. Removing the border does not significantly increase the chart area. The benefit is reducing clutter by removing an element that adds no informative value.

opt_nothing.message: Not quite. Borders are not necessary to define chart boundaries. White space is enough to separate the chart from surrounding content, and removing the border reduces clutter.

correct.message: Exactly. Borders add no informative value. White space is sufficient to separate the chart from surrounding content.

incorrect.message: Think about whether the border adds information or just decoration. White space can do the job of separating the chart.

hints: Does the border tell the audience anything about the data?
White space can separate the chart from surrounding content without needing a border.

public.prompt: Three slides from the Lagos presentation are shown out of order. Which order places them correctly into opening–body–call to action?

options.text: Slide A (context/situation) → Slide B (finding + evidence) → Slide C (call to action)
Slide B (finding + evidence) → Slide A (context/situation) → Slide C (call to action)
Slide C (call to action) → Slide A (context/situation) → Slide B (finding + evidence)
Slide A (context/situation) → Slide C (call to action) → Slide B (finding + evidence)

opt_context_finding_action.message: Correct. A presentation should have an obvious beginning (context/situation), middle (finding + evidence), and end (call to action).

opt_finding_context_action.message: Not quite. The beginning should establish the context of the situation before presenting findings. Starting with findings leaves the audience without necessary background.

opt_action_context_finding.message: Not quite. The call to action should come at the end, after the context and findings have been established. Starting with the request leaves the audience unprepared.

opt_context_action_finding.message: Not quite. The call to action should come at the end, after the findings have been presented. Placing it before the findings means the audience has not yet seen the evidence supporting the request.

correct.message: Right. The structure is opening (context), body (finding + evidence), and call to action (what is being asked).

incorrect.message: Remember the three-part structure: beginning (context), middle (finding + evidence), end (call to action).

hints: The beginning should establish the context before presenting findings.
The call to action comes at the end, after the evidence has been presented.

public.prompt: Drag the five Lagos presentation elements into the correct opening–body–call-to-action order.

items.text: QuickShip's Lagos operations have grown 40% in the past year
40% of deliveries now exceed the 60-minute target

correct.message: Perfect. You organized the elements into the correct structure: opening (context + problem), body (evidence + solution), and call to action (request).

incorrect.message: Think about the three-part structure. The opening establishes context, the body presents findings and evidence, and the end states what is being asked.

hints: Start with context to establish the situation.
Present the problem and evidence in the middle.
End with the solution and what you are asking for.

public.prompt: Four executive summary drafts are shown. Which one best follows the taught structure?

options.text: Draft A: Has a takeaway title, uses section headers ('Finding' and 'Recommendation'), and presents content in prose paragraphs
Draft B: Has a descriptive title, uses bullet points throughout, and covers findings and recommendations
Draft C: Has a takeaway title and prose paragraphs, but no section headers to distinguish findings from recommendations
Draft D: Has section headers and prose, but runs to four pages with extensive detail

opt_structured.message: Correct. An executive summary should have a takeaway title, section headers to group content into easily-discernible sections, and prose paragraphs rather than bullets.

opt_bullets.message: Not quite. While bullet points are common, the taught structure uses prose paragraphs with section headers. Bullets can make the summary feel like a list rather than a narrative.

opt_no_headers.message: Not quite. Section headers are important for grouping content into easily-discernible sections. Without them, the reader has to work harder to distinguish findings from recommendations.

opt_long.message: Not quite. An executive summary should be a one- or two-page overview, not four pages. The goal is to provide a concise summary, not extensive detail.

correct.message: Right. The executive summary structure includes a takeaway title, section headers, and prose paragraphs — all within one or two pages.

incorrect.message: Remember the key elements: a takeaway title, section headers to group content, prose paragraphs, and a one- or two-page length.

hints: Section headers help the reader quickly identify findings and recommendations.
Prose paragraphs create a narrative arc rather than a list.
An executive summary should be concise — one or two pages.

public.instruction:
Using the Lagos scenario below, write a three-sentence executive summary with a title stating the main takeaway, a 'Finding' section, and a 'Recommendation' section. Your summary should:
• Have a title that states the main takeaway
• Include a 'Finding' section header followed by one sentence describing the delivery-time problem
• Include a 'Recommendation' section header followed by one sentence proposing the second hub
• Use prose (not bullets)
• Be concise (approximately 50–75 words total)

rubric.criterion: Title states main takeaway (e.g., 'Second Lagos Hub Needed to Meet Delivery Targets')
Includes a 'Finding' section header followed by a sentence describing the delivery-time problem
Includes a 'Recommendation' section header followed by a sentence proposing the second hub
Uses prose paragraphs rather than bullet points
The summary is concise (approximately 50–75 words) and focused on the key points

correct.message: Excellent work. Your executive summary follows the taught structure with a takeaway title, section headers, and prose paragraphs.

incorrect.message: Review the structure: a takeaway title, 'Finding' and 'Recommendation' section headers, and prose paragraphs (not bullets).

hints: Start with a title that states the main takeaway, not just a description.
Use section headers ('Finding' and 'Recommendation') to organize your content.
